completion.text:
When Tommy set forth on the trail of the two men, it took all Tuppence's self-command to refrain from accompanying him. However, she was consoled by the reflection that her reasoning had been justified by events: that one slender thread of the name "Rita" had set the Young Adventurers once more upon the track of the abductors of Jane Finn.

The question was what to do next? Tuppence hated letting the grass grow under her feet. She retraced her steps to the entrance hall of the mansions. It was now tenanted by a small lift-boy, who was polishing brass fittings and whistling the latest air with a good deal of vigour.

"Well, William," she remarked cheerfully, in the best approved hospital-early-morning style, "getting a good shine up?"

The boy grinned responsively. "Albert, miss," he corrected.

"Albert be it," said Tuppence. "Look! Do you know what this is?" With a dramatic gesture she flung back the left side of her coat and exposed a small enamelled badge. It would have been fatal for her plans had Albert known it, since the badge was the device of a local training corps originated by the archdeacon in the early days of the war. But Tuppence had sharp eyes, and had noted the corner of a threepenny detective novel protruding from Albert's pocket.

"American Detective Force!" she hissed.

Albert fell for it. "Lord!" he murmured ecstatically.

Tuppence nodded and jerked a thumb up the stairs. "No. 20. Calls herself Vandemeyer. Vandemeyer! Ha! ha!"

"A crook?" Albert queried eagerly.

"A crook? I should say so. Ready Rita they call her in the States."

"Ready Rita," repeated Albert deliriously. "Oh, ain't it just like the pictures!"

It was. Tuppence was a great frequenter of the cinema.

"Annie always said as how she was a bad lot," continued the boy. Annie, it appeared, was the house-parlourmaid. She was leaving to-day after a regular turn up with her mistress.

That, Tuppence explained, was what they were after Mrs. Vandemeyer for: the emeralds of Rysdale, the oil king. "Worth a million dollars!"

An idea was dawning in Tuppence's brain. "See here, son, my brain's got busy. How would it be if you mentioned that you'd got a young cousin, or a friend of yours had, that might suit the place. You get me?"

"I'm there," said Albert instantly. "You leave it to me, miss, and I'll fix the whole thing up in two ticks."

"Some lad!" commented Tuppence. "You let me know, and if it's O.K. I'll be round to-morrow at eleven o'clock."

"Where am I to let you know to?"

"_Ritz_," replied Tuppence laconically. "Name of Cowley."

"Don't fret, son," drawled Tuppence. "If this goes well, you shall come in on the ground floor."

With which promise she took leave of her new ally, well pleased with her morning's work.

She went straight back to the _Ritz_ and wrote a few brief words to Mr. Carter. She then started off on a shopping expedition that began at a cheap clothing store and finished at a well-known hairdresser's. With an actress's pencil she slightly altered the line of her eyebrows. Taken with the new luxuriant growth of fair hair above, this so changed her appearance that she felt confident that even Whittington would not recognize her. The cap and apron would be an even more valuable disguise. From hospital experience she knew only too well that a nurse out of uniform is frequently unrecognized by her patients.

Dinner was a solitary meal. Tuppence was rather surprised at Tommy's non-return. Julius, too, was absent, but that was more easily explained.

"This is very dull for _me!_" thought Tuppence. "Here I am bursting with news, and absolutely no one to tell it to! I wonder where Tommy is."

The morning brought a note from Mr. Carter:

"DEAR MISS TUPPENCE,

"You have made a splendid start, and I congratulate you. Those people are absolutely desperate and incapable of either mercy or pity. I warn you again that I can promise you no protection. If you choose to withdraw now no one could blame you.

"If, in spite of my warnings, you make up your mind to go through with it, you will find everything arranged. You have lived for two years with Miss Dufferin, The Parsonage, Llanelly, and Mrs. Vandemeyer can apply to her for a reference.

"Stick as near to the truth as possible--it minimizes the danger of 'slips.' I suggest that you should represent yourself to be what you are, a former V.A.D., who has chosen domestic service as a profession. That explains away any incongruities of voice or manner.

"Whichever way you decide, good luck to you.

"Your sincere friend,

"MR. CARTER."

Tuppence's spirits rose mercurially. Mr. Carter's warnings passed unheeded. With some reluctance she abandoned the interesting part she had sketched out for herself. She had too much common sense not to recognize the force of Mr. Carter's arguments.

There was still no word from Tommy, but the morning post brought a somewhat dirty postcard with the words "It's O.K." scrawled upon it.

At ten-thirty Tuppence drove to Paddington with a slightly battered tin trunk containing her new possessions, and left it in the cloak room. Ten minutes later a metamorphosed Tuppence walked demurely out of the station and entered a bus.

It was a few minutes past eleven when she again entered the hall of South Audley Mansions. Albert did not immediately recognize her. When he did, his admiration was unbounded.

"Blest if I'd have known you! That rig-out's top-hole."

"Glad you like it, Albert," replied Tuppence modestly. "By the way, am I your cousin, or am I not?"

"Your voice too," cried the delighted boy. "It's as English as anything! No, I said as a friend of mine knew a young gal."

As Tuppence rang the bell of No. 20, a smart young woman opened the door.

"I've come about the place," said Tuppence.

"It's a rotten place," said the young woman without hesitation. "Regular old cat--always interfering. There's never anything in the waste-paper basket--she burns everything. She's a wrong 'un, that's what she is. Cook knows something about her--but she won't tell--scared to death of her. And suspicious! She's on to you in a minute if you as much as speak to a fellow. I can tell you----"

But what more Annie could tell, Tuppence was never destined to learn. At that moment a clear voice with a peculiarly steely ring to it called:

"Annie!"

The smart young woman jumped as if she had been shot. "Yes, ma'am."

"Who are you talking to?"

"It's a young woman about the situation, ma'am."

"Show her in then. At once."

Tuppence was ushered into a room on the right of the long passage. A woman was standing by the fireplace. She was no longer in her first youth, and the beauty she undeniably possessed was hardened and coarsened. Her eyes, of a piercing electric blue, seemed to possess a faculty of boring into the very soul of the person she was looking at. And yet, despite her swaying grace, you felt instinctively the presence of something hard and menacing. It was a kind of metallic strength that found expression in the tones of her voice and in that gimlet-like quality of her eyes.

For the first time Tuppence felt afraid. She had not feared Whittington, but this woman was different. Mr. Carter's warning recurred to her mind. Here, indeed, she might expect no mercy.

Fighting down the panic that urged her to turn tail and run, Tuppence returned the lady's gaze firmly and respectfully.

"You can sit down. How did you hear I wanted a house-parlourmaid?"

"Through a friend who knows the lift boy here. He thought the place might suit me."

"You speak like an educated girl?"

Glibly enough, Tuppence ran through her imaginary career on the lines suggested by Mr. Carter. It seemed to her that the tension of Mrs. Vandemeyer's attitude relaxed.

"I see," Mrs. Vandemeyer remarked at length. "Is there anyone I can write to for a reference?"

"I lived last with a Miss Dufferin, The Parsonage, Llanelly. I was with her two years."

"And then you thought you would get more money by coming to London, I suppose? Well, it doesn't matter to me. I will give you £50--£60--whatever you want. You can come in at once?"

"Yes, ma'am. To-day, if you like. My box is at Paddington."

"Go and fetch it in a taxi, then. By the way, what's your name?"

"Prudence Cooper, ma'am."

"Very well, Prudence. Go away and fetch your box. I shall be out to lunch. The cook will show you where everything is."

"Thank you, ma'am."

Tuppence withdrew and passed meekly out.

The adventure had begun, but she felt less elated than she had done earlier in the morning. It crossed her mind that if the unknown Jane Finn had fallen into the hands of Mrs. Vandemeyer, it was likely to have gone hard with her.
